{{Short description|Numerical method for solving stochastic differential equations}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Milstein method''' is a technique for the approximate [[numerical analysis|numerical solution]] of a [[stochastic differential equation]]. It is named after [[Grigori Milstein]] who first published it in 1974.<ref>{{cite journal|first=G. N.|last=Mil'shtein |title=Приближенное интегрирование стохастических дифференциальных уравнений |trans-title=Approximate integration of stochastic differential equations|journal=Teoriya Veroyatnostei i ee Primeneniya|volume=19|issue=3|year=1974| pages=583–588| url =http://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=tvp&paperid=2929&option_lang=eng|language=ru}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Mil’shtein | first1 = G. N. | title = Approximate Integration of Stochastic Differential Equations | doi = 10.1137/1119062 | journal = Theory of Probability & Its Applications | volume = 19 | issue = 3 | pages = 557–000 | year = 1975 }}</ref>

==Description==
Consider the [[autonomous equation|autonomous]] [[Itō calculus|Itō]] stochastic differential equation:
<math display="block">\mathrm{d} X_t = a(X_t) \, \mathrm{d} t + b(X_t) \, \mathrm{d} W_t</math>
with [[initial condition]] <math>X_{0} = x_{0}</math>, where <math>W_{t}</math> denotes the [[Wiener process]], and suppose that we wish to solve this SDE on some interval of time&nbsp;<math>[0,T]</math>. Then the '''Milstein approximation''' to the true solution <math>X</math> is the [[Markov chain]] <math>Y</math> defined as follows:

* Partition the interval <math>[0,T]</math> into <math>N</math> equal subintervals of width <math>\Delta t>0</math>: <math display="block">0 = \tau_0 < \tau_1 < \dots < \tau_N = T\text{ with }\tau_n:=n\Delta t\text{ and }\Delta t = \frac{T}{N}</math>
* Set <math>Y_0 = x_0;</math>
* Recursively define <math>Y_n</math> for <math>1 \leq n \leq N</math> by: <math display="block">Y_{n + 1} = Y_n + a(Y_n) \Delta t + b(Y_n) \Delta W_n + \frac{1}{2} b(Y_n) b'(Y_n) \left( (\Delta W_n)^2 - \Delta t \right)</math> where <math>b'</math> denotes the [[derivative]] of <math>b(x)</math> with respect to <math>x</math> and: <math display="block">\Delta W_n = W_{\tau_{n + 1}} - W_{\tau_n}</math> are [[independent and identically distributed]] [[normal distribution|normal random variables]] with [[expected value]] zero and [[variance]] <math>\Delta t</math>. Then <math>Y_n</math> will approximate <math>X_{\tau_n}</math> for <math>0 \leq n \leq N</math>, and increasing <math>N</math> will yield a better approximation.

Note that when <math> b'(Y_n) = 0 </math> (i.e. the diffusion term does not depend on <math>X_{t}</math>) this method is equivalent to the [[Euler–Maruyama method]].

The Milstein scheme has both weak and strong order of convergence <math>\Delta t</math> which is superior to the [[Euler–Maruyama method]], which in turn has the same weak order of convergence <math>\Delta t</math> but inferior strong order of convergence <math>\sqrt{\Delta t}</math>.<ref>{{cite book |first=V. |last=Mackevičius |title=Introduction to Stochastic Analysis |publisher=Wiley |year=2011 |isbn=978-1-84821-311-1 }}</ref>

== Intuitive derivation ==

For this derivation, we will only look at [[geometric Brownian motion]] (GBM), the stochastic differential equation of which is given by:
<math display="block">\mathrm{d} X_t = \mu X \mathrm{d} t + \sigma X d W_t</math>
with real constants <math>\mu</math> and <math>\sigma</math>. Using [[Itō's lemma]] we get:
<math display="block">\mathrm{d}\ln X_t= \left(\mu - \frac{1}{2} \sigma^2\right)\mathrm{d}t+\sigma\mathrm{d}W_t</math>

Thus, the solution to the GBM SDE is:
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
X_{t+\Delta t}&=X_t\exp\left\{\int_t^{t+\Delta t}\left(\mu-\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right)\mathrm{d}t+\int_t^{t+\Delta t}\sigma\mathrm{d}W_u\right\} \\
&\approx X_t\left(1+\mu\Delta t-\frac{1}{2} \sigma^2\Delta t+\sigma\Delta W_t+\frac{1}{2}\sigma^2(\Delta W_t)^2\right) \\
&= X_t + a(X_t)\Delta t+b(X_t)\Delta W_t+\frac{1}{2}b(X_t)b'(X_t)((\Delta W_t)^2-\Delta t)
\end{align}</math>
where
<math display="block"> a(x) = \mu x, ~b(x) = \sigma x </math>

The numerical solution is presented in the graphic for three different trajectories.<ref>{{cite web |first=Umberto |last=Picchini |title=SDE Toolbox: simulation and estimation of stochastic differential equations with Matlab |url=https://sdetoolbox.sourceforge.net/ }}</ref>

=== Computer implementation ===
The following [[Python (programming language)|Python]] code implements the Milstein method and uses it to solve the SDE describing geometric Brownian motion defined by
<math display="block">\begin{cases}
dY_t= \mu Y \, {\mathrm d}t + \sigma Y \, {\mathrm d}W_t \\
Y_0=Y_\text{init}
\end{cases}</math>

<syntaxhighlight lang="numpy" line="1">
# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
# Milstein Method

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


class Model:
    """Stochastic model constants."""
    mu = 3
    sigma = 1


def dW(dt):
    """Random sample normal distribution."""
    return np.random.normal(loc=0.0, scale=np.sqrt(dt))


def run_simulation():
    """ Return the result of one full simulation."""
    # One second and thousand grid points
    T_INIT = 0
    T_END = 1
    N = 1000 # Compute 1000 grid points
    DT = float(T_END - T_INIT) / N
    TS = np.arange(T_INIT, T_END + DT, DT)

    Y_INIT = 1

    # Vectors to fill
    ys = np.zeros(N + 1)
    ys[0] = Y_INIT
    for i in range(1, TS.size):
        t = (i - 1) * DT
        y = ys[i - 1]
        dw = dW(DT)

        # Sum up terms as in the Milstein method
        ys[i] = y + \
            Model.mu * y * DT + \
            Model.sigma * y * dw + \
            (Model.sigma**2 / 2) * y * (dw**2 - DT)

    return TS, ys


def plot_simulations(num_sims: int):
    """Plot several simulations in one image."""
    for _ in range(num_sims):
        plt.plot(*run_simulation())

    plt.xlabel("time (s)")
    plt.ylabel("y")
    plt.grid()
    plt.show()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    NUM_SIMS = 2
    plot_simulations(NUM_SIMS)

</syntaxhighlight>
